document.title: Work Update — July 25, 2026
document.headline: Work Queue 2.0 moved from concept to a working functional beta.

workCoverage.coverageDescription: Covers the July 25, 2026 design, construction, testing, and launch of Work Queue 2.0 as a functional beta, including shared location architecture, operational data structures, modular Apps Script services, backend-first testing, interface construction, end-to-end lifecycle verification, creation of a real task, retry-safe error handling, deferred photo support, and preparation of ten starter task templates.

subject.mainFocus: Designing, building, testing, and launching Work Queue 2.0 as a functional beta with a complete task lifecycle, shared location architecture, modular backend, polished interface, visible user feedback, and starter task templates.
subject.description: Klinswork work update for July 25, 2026, covering the design, construction, testing, launch, and next development phase of Work Queue 2.0.

narrative.promptingSituation: The older Tasker application was not a suitable base for continued incremental repair, and the new system needed a clearer scope, shared data ownership, reliable lifecycle rules, permanent history, and a practical interface.
narrative.initialUnderstanding: The strongest path was to define Work Queue 2.0 as a separate project, establish shared location and operational data structures first, then prove the backend before introducing browser complexity.
narrative.intendedOutcome: Launch a functional beta capable of creating, starting, annotating, completing, reopening, and re-completing tasks while preserving all activity.
narrative.approach: Define scope and data ownership, create shared location and operational sheets, divide the backend into focused services, test the lifecycle directly in Apps Script, build the browser interface, repeat the lifecycle through the interface, create a realistic task, verify recovery from a real connection error, and prepare the next template-assisted phase.

keyDecisions.decision: Replace Tasker rather than repair it incrementally.
keyDecisions.reason: Work Queue required a different scope, architecture, data model, and workflow.
consequences: The older deployment remained as a fallback while Work Queue developed separately.

keyDecisions.decision: Keep every task action as a new activity record.
keyDecisions.reason: Operational history should remain complete and auditable.
consequences: Creation, notes, transitions, completion, and reopening remain chronologically visible.

keyDecisions.decision: Test the backend before launching the interface.
keyDecisions.reason: This isolates service and data problems from browser and deployment complexity.
consequences: Failures became easier to localize and interface work began on a proven service layer.

keyDecisions.reason: The core workflow should remain stable and focused before adding upload complexity.
alternativesConsidered: Add image capture in the first beta
consequences: Photo support remained a future feature rather than a risk to the initial launch.

narrative.methodEstablished: Define data and ownership first, build focused services, test the backend lifecycle directly, expose startup data, construct the interface, repeat the lifecycle through the browser, and prove the system with a realistic task.
narrative.result: Work Queue 2.0 became a functional beta with eight shared units, 163 active locations, a complete task lifecycle, permanent activity history, a polished interface, retry-safe feedback, and ten prepared task templates.
lessonsLearned: Backend-first testing reduces uncertainty before browser integration.
Visible feedback is part of application functionality.
Retry-safe forms should preserve user-entered content after connection failures.
Shared reference data prevents multiple applications from maintaining conflicting copies.
A realistic end-to-end task is stronger evidence than isolated function tests alone.

sections.title: Application scope and architecture
sections.contentSummary: We began by deciding that the existing Tasker app should be replaced rather than incrementally repaired. Before writing code, we defined Work Queue 2.0's purpose, boundaries, workflow, data ownership, and relationship to the wider Klinswork tool system. Create tasks directly inside the application. Remove the old Google Form intake. Eliminate the Recommendations feature. Separate active work from completed work. Keep Work Queue compatible with other Klinswork tools. Build it as a separate project so the older Tasker deployment could remain online during development.

sections.title: Shared location architecture
sections.contentSummary: A centralized location directory was designed before the task system itself. This prevents Inventory 3.0, Work Queue, and future scheduling tools from maintaining separate copies of the same location data. Shared directory Klinswork_Locations became the common reference source for units, rooms, offices, restrooms, common areas, and other work locations. Completed coverage 8 units 163 active Work Queue locations Application-specific enablement Reusable parent-and-child relationships This was also one of the first major uses of direct spreadsheet generation and editing, substantially reducing repetitive setup work.

sections.title: Operational data structure
sections.contentSummary: A separate spreadsheet was created for Work Queue 2.0 operational data. Tasks Stores each task's current state, including ID, status, priority, category, location, description, assignee, timestamps, completion note, and archived state. Task_Activity Stores the full chronological history of task creation, starts, notes, completions, reopenings, and later changes. Settings Stores app version, default priority, completion-note requirements, notification settings, and location cache duration. Task_Templates Provides the foundation for reusable task choices that reduce typing during task creation.

projectRelevance.primaryProjectContribution: Documents the Work Queue 2.0 contribution: Operational data structure.

sections.title: Modular Apps Script backend
sections.contentSummary: The backend was divided into focused files rather than written as one large script. Config.gs Spreadsheet IDs, sheet names, app name, version, and configuration. Code.gs Setup, diagnostics, and backend test functions. WebApp.gs Web app entry point and startup data. Validation.gs Configuration, schema, input, status, and transition validation. Utilities.gs IDs, dates, formatting, normalization, sorting, and user attribution. LocationService.gs Shared location retrieval and unit/location resolution. TaskService.gs Complete task lifecycle, spreadsheet persistence, and activity logging.

projectRelevance.primaryProjectContribution: Documents the Work Queue 2.0 contribution: Modular Apps Script backend.

sections.title: Backend-first testing
sections.contentSummary: One of the most valuable process improvements of the day was testing the backend directly through Apps Script → Run → test function before launching the interface. Tests covered spreadsheet setup, schema validation, location retrieval, task creation, notes, status transitions, activity history, and startup data. Startup summary App: Work Queue 2.0 8 units 163 locations Default priority: Normal Why this mattered It isolated backend problems before introducing browser JavaScript, interface rendering, deployment versions, filters, and modals.

sections.title: Interface and user feedback
sections.contentSummary: The application interface was created in Dashboard.html , Styles.html , and Scripts.html . Interface structure Branded header and summary cards Active Work and Completed Work tabs Filters, task cards, and detail modals Activity timeline and action forms Confirmation dialog and toast notifications Visible feedback Loading spinners Busy button labels such as “Saving...” Green success messages Inline error messages Empty-state guidance Retry-safe forms

sections.title: Lifecycle testing through the interface
sections.contentSummary: After the backend passed independently, the same task lifecycle was repeated through the actual web interface. Opened Completed Work. Displayed the backend test task. Opened the task-detail modal. Displayed the entire activity history. Reopened the task. Added notes. Completed it again. Confirmed that earlier events remained intact.

projectRelevance.primaryProjectContribution: Documents the Work Queue 2.0 contribution: Lifecycle testing through the interface.

sections.title: Created and completed a real task
sections.contentSummary: A new task was created entirely through the interface using a selected unit, selected location, free-text category, free-text assignee, description, initial note, and normal priority. The interface correctly: Changed the button label while saving. Saved the task to the spreadsheet. Displayed a green success notification. Refreshed the task collections. Opened the new task automatically. Displayed its task ID and metadata. Recorded creation and the initial note as separate activities. Moved the task into Completed Work after completion.

sections.title: Real error handling
sections.contentSummary: During one completion attempt, the browser experienced an HTTP 0 connection failure. This became a useful real-world test of the app's recovery behavior. The app did correctly Displayed the failure visibly. Did not falsely report success. Preserved the completion note. Allowed the user to retry. After retry The task completed successfully. The task moved into Completed Work. The task history remained intact.

sections.contentSummary: A later version may allow users to photograph either the condition being reported or the work after completion. Snap a photo directly from a phone. Choose an existing image. This feature was intentionally deferred so the current workflow could remain stable and focused.

sections.contentSummary: Repeated housekeeping tasks should require minimal typing. email.subject: Work Queue 2.0 Functional Beta Update
email.body: Work Queue 2.0 has moved from concept to a functioning beta. It now supports task creation, starting, notes, completion, reopening, and permanent activity history across eight units and 163 active locations. The complete lifecycle was tested through both the backend and the web interface, including a real task and recovery from a connection failure. The next immediate step is connecting the prepared task templates to the New Task form.
